recommendation_text: Non-curative surgery is offered to patients who are considered incurable. It can be semi-classified into either palliative surgery or reduction surgery depending on the aim of surgery.

breadcrumb: Surgery/Types and definitions of gastric surgery/Non-curative surgery/Palliative surgery
recommendation_text: Serious symptoms such as bleeding or obstruction may develop in a patient with advanced/metastatic gastric cancer. Surgery to relieve imminent symptoms may then be considered an option, and palliative gastrectomy or gastrojejunostomy is selected depending on the resectability of the primary tumor and/or surgical risks.

breadcrumb: Surgery/Types and definitions of gastric surgery/Non-curative surgery/Reduction surgery
recommendation_text: Reduction surgery is defined as gastrectomy performed for patients with incurable factors such as unresectable liver metastasis and peritoneal metastasis, with no tumor-associated symptoms such as bleeding, obstruction, and pain. It aims to prolong survival or to delay the onset of symptoms by reducing tumor volume.

recommendation_text: However, an international, cooperative, randomized, controlled trial (REGATTA, JCOG0705/KGCA01) failed to prove a survival benefit of reduction surgery [5]. source_name: Japanese gastric cancer treatment guidelines 2025 (7th edition)

recommendation_text: Postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy is delivered with the intention to reduce recurrence by controlling residual tumor cells after curative resection. As adjuvant chemotherapy, the efficacy of S-1 was proven in 2006 by the ACTS-GC trial [85, 86], a study that secured the place of postoperative S-1 monotherapy as a standard of care.

recommendation_text: The CLASSIC trial conducted in Korea, China, and Taiwan showed the prolongation of relapse-free survival by capecitabine plus oxaliplatin therapy (CapeOx) for TNM Stage II/III gastric cancer [87], and a study conducted in Japan confirmed its safety in Japanese patients [88].

recommendation_text: A combination of S-1 and docetaxel was shown to have significant benefit for relapse-free survival over S-1 alone for Stage III gastric cancer in the JACCRO GC-07 trial [89].

recommendation_text: In the phase III ARTIST2 trial of adjuvant chemotherapy for postoperative stage (pStage) II/III with D2 dissection in Korea, S-1 plus oxaliplatin (SOX) therapy significantly prolonged disease-free survival, the primary endpoint, compared with S-1 [90].

recommendation_text: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is premised on “curative resection” based on diagnostic imaging. recommendation_text: Though a wealth of experience in postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy has been accumulated in Japan, there are still not a few cases for whom it is difficult to perform intensive adjuvant chemotherapy due to decreased oral intake and complications.

recommendation_text: Since postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy targets patients who have undergone curative resection, the indication can be accurately determined based on histological findings, but the indication for preoperative adjuvant chemotherapy is determined based on diagnostic imaging.

recommendation_text: A disadvantage of neoadjuvant chemotherapy is that some overdiagnosed cases who actually have early cancer not requiring peri-operative chemotherapy and underdiagnosed cases who actually have unresectable peritoneal metastases not detected by conventional imaging examination can be included as targets of neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

recommendation_text: There are also further disadvantages, such as the risk of becoming unresectable due to progression during chemotherapy and increased postoperative complications. recommendation_text: Thus, safety issues in terms of adverse events during chemotherapy and incidence of postoperative morbidity, accuracy of pretreatment staging, incidence of unresectable disease due to progression during neoadjuvant treatment, and QOL should be analyzed in future neoadjuvant trials in addition to proving superiority in survival outcomes over standar
